series.title: Working-age (under 65) 'Some College, No Credential' population
series.source_name: National Student Clearinghouse Research Center, Some College, No Credential: 2025 Report
series.notes: 37.6M (under 65) and 43.1M (all ages) are stated on the report and landing page. Prior-year points are DERIVED by subtracting the stated year-over-year increases (+799,000 or +2.2% for 2022-23 to 2023-24; '+1 million, +2.9%' for 2021-22 to 2022-23), so they are rounded approximations; use 37.6 as the only stated level. 2.1M people newly stopped out Jan 2022 to Jul 2023, vs 956,000 who re-enrolled or earned a credential in 2022-23 and 418,000 who aged out. Latest edition is June 2025 (data as of start of 2023-24); NSC lists the next edition for November 2026, not yet seen.

series.title: Share of entering degree/certificate-seeking undergraduates (all entry types) who completed an award at the same institution within 6 years, 2015-16 entry cohort, by Pell status
series.source_name: NCES Digest of Education Statistics 2024, Table 326.27 (IPEDS Outcome Measures)
series.notes: Includes first-time and transfer-in, full- and part-time entrants. Pell status = Pell disbursed in first year. Awards conferred by the reporting institution only, so students who transferred and finished elsewhere count as non-completers. At public 2-year colleges Pell recipients complete slightly MORE often than non-Pell. All-4-year 6-year rate for this cohort: 52.5%; all-2-year: 30.5%. Pell is the best available national proxy for family income in IPEDS.

series.title: Median usual weekly earnings and unemployment rate by educational attainment, 2025
series.source_name: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Projections, 'Education pays' table (CPS)

categories.label: Less than a high school diploma

series.notes: Persons age 25+; earnings are for full-time wage and salary workers. 2025 annual figures are 11-month averages excluding October 2025 (not collected during the federal shutdown), so not strictly comparable with prior years. 'Some college, no degree' earns $96/week (about 10%) more than high school only, vs $612/week (63%) for a bachelor's (derived).

series.title: Annual wages of early-career workers (age 22-27), full-time, constant 2025 dollars
series.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates (wages, released Feb 4, 2026)
series.notes: Bachelor's degree only (not graduate degrees) vs high school diploma only, ages 22-27, full-time, excluding current students. CPS March Supplement via IPUMS. The Fed notes part of the gap may reflect differences in aptitude. 2025 values are round numbers as published. Landing page: https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/college-labor-market

series.title: Early-career college wage premium: median bachelor's vs median high school wage, ages 22-27
series.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates (derived)
series.notes: DERIVED by dividing the two published medians in the NY Fed wages file. Premium ranged 34% to 55% in 1990-2010 and 47% to 69% in 2011-2025 (noisy year to year; a 3-year average is advisable for charting); it was 39% in 1990 and 50% in 2025 (60,000 vs 40,000). This is an early-career premium only; it is not a causal estimate.

series.title: Unemployment rate: recent college graduates vs young workers vs all workers (annual mean of monthly values)
series.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates (Nov 2, 2026 release, data through 2026:Q3)
series.notes: Annual figures are my simple means of the published monthly series, which the Fed already seasonally adjusts and smooths with a 3-month moving average; 2026 covers Jan-Sep. Recent graduates = age 22-27 with bachelor's or higher; young workers = age 22-27 without a bachelor's; all workers = 16-65; college grads = 22-65. Latest monthly: recent grads 5.2% (Sep 2026) vs young workers 7.4%, all workers 4.0%. Since 2019 recent grads have been ABOVE the all-worker rate but still below young non-graduates.

series.title: Underemployment rate (working in jobs that typically do not require a degree), annual mean of monthly values
series.source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates
series.notes: Same averaging method as unemployment series. Latest monthly (Sep 2026): recent grads 42.5%, all grads 33.7%.

series.title: Cost as a reason for not being enrolled, unenrolled U.S. adults 18-59 without a degree
series.source_name: Lumina Foundation-Gallup, Cost of College report (2024 State of Higher Education study)

categories.label: Cost 'very important' reason not enrolled (all unenrolled)
Value of further education 'very important' reason
Enrolled students who considered stopping out citing cost

series.notes: Exact question: 'How important are each of the following as reasons why you are not currently enrolled?' Item: 'The cost of the degree or credential program' (very / moderately / not very / not at all important). Fieldwork Oct 9 to Nov 16, 2023; web survey of 14,032 (6,015 enrolled, 5,012 stopped out, 3,005 never enrolled) via Dynata non-probability opt-in panel, weighted to U.S. adults 18-59 with a HS diploma but no degree. Cost led all tested factors by at least 10 points. Demand side from the 2025 study (https://www.gallup.com/file/analytics/660188/Gallup-Lumina%20Foundation-State%20of%20Higher%20Education%202025_Report.pdf): 57% of unenrolled adults considered pursuing a degree or credential in the past two years (59% in 2023); fieldwork Oct 2-31, 2024.

caveats: Earnings gaps by education are associations, not causal returns; selection (ability, family background) explains part of the gap. The NY Fed says so explicitly on its wage chart.
BLS 2025 annual averages exclude October 2025 (not collected during the federal shutdown) and are not strictly comparable to earlier years.

NCES Table 326.10 and 326.27 count only completion at the first/reporting institution, which understates completion for transfer students; NSC counts completion anywhere. Do not mix the two on one chart without labeling.

Table 326.27 Pell figures cover ALL entering students (first-time and transfer, full- and part-time), not just first-time full-time. Pell is a proxy for low family income; NCES does not publish a national family-income completion series in these tables.
NSC income breakdown is by NEIGHBORHOOD income quintile, not family income.

SCNC prior-year levels (35.8M, 36.8M) are derived from stated changes, not stated levels. NSC also revises its SCNC methodology between editions, so earlier report editions are not directly comparable.
NSC and IPEDS enrollment counts differ in scope; the NCES series ends at fall 2023 and the NSC figure is for fall 2025.
NY Fed annual values are my means of already-smoothed monthly data; 2026 covers January to September only. The wage premium series is my ratio of two published medians.
Time-to-degree (2015-16 graduates) and student employment (2020, pandemic year) are the latest national figures found on primary pages but are dated.

Gallup-Lumina samples come from a non-probability opt-in web panel (Dynata) of adults 18-59 with a HS diploma and no degree, weighted to ACS demographics; no conventional margin of error applies. The 2025 report's charts of reasons are images, so the cost figures used here come from the 2024 study (fieldwork fall 2023).
CEW lifetime earnings are from 2021 using 2009-2019 ACS data and full-time, full-year workers only, which excludes those out of work.
Census Table A-2 uses 'completed 4 years of college or more', now measured as bachelor's degree or higher.
